paras.A: Sleep researchers have long known that teenagers need around nine hours of sleep a night, yet surveys in many countries suggest that most get fewer than seven. This gap is not simply the result of laziness or late-night entertainment, as parents often assume. Biological changes during adolescence play a larger part than most people realise, and schools, perhaps unintentionally, make the problem worse.
paras.B: During puberty, the internal body clock shifts. Hormones that make us feel sleepy are released about two hours later in teenagers than in children or adults. A fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten o'clock may therefore lie awake for hours, not because of a mobile phone, but because the body is not yet ready for sleep. The same clock makes it hard to wake early, which explains why many teenagers seem unusually tired in the first lessons of the morning.
paras.C: Most schools, however, start early. In several American districts, classes begin before half past seven, and students who live far from school must get up before dawn. When a group of schools in Minnesota moved the start of the day by an hour, researchers recorded fewer absences, better exam results and a fall in road accidents involving young drivers. Not every district has copied the experiment. Transport timetables, sports practice and parents' working hours all make later starts difficult to organise.
paras.D: Technology complicates the picture. Light from screens delays the release of sleep hormones, and notifications interrupt rest even after the phone has been put aside. Some families now keep devices in the kitchen overnight. Evidence for this approach is mixed: it helps younger teenagers, who accept the rule, but older ones often find a way round it. Researchers who have studied the problem believe that education may be more effective than prohibition, since teenagers who understand why they feel tired are more willing to change their habits.
paras.E: The consequences of poor sleep extend beyond tiredness. Studies link short sleep in adolescence to difficulties with concentration, low mood and, over time, a higher risk of weight gain. Some scientists caution, though, that most of this evidence shows correlation rather than cause: unhappy teenagers may sleep badly, rather than the other way round. What is clear is that sleep is not wasted time. During the night, the brain sorts the day's information and stores what is important, which is why students who revise late and sleep little often remember less than those who stop earlier.
paras.F: Families and schools can respond in practical ways. Parents can agree a regular bedtime with their teenage children rather than impose one, since rules that young people help to make are more likely to be followed. A short walk outdoors in the morning exposes the eyes to natural light, which helps to move the body clock earlier. Weekend lie-ins of more than two hours, on the other hand, make the next Monday harder. Doctors also recommend avoiding caffeine after lunch, because its effects can last far longer than most people expect.
paras.G: Countries differ in how seriously they take the problem. In parts of Australia and France, health ministries have published guidance on school timetables, while in others the issue is left entirely to individual head teachers. Researchers argue that national data would help, because it is difficult to compare schools whose pupils differ in age, income and distance from home. Until such information exists, the debate is likely to continue, with each side able to quote a study that supports its case.

paras.A: By 2050, about two-thirds of the world's population is expected to live in cities, and feeding all these people will be a major challenge. Traditional farming needs large areas of land, and most of it lies far from urban centres. Food must therefore be transported hundreds of kilometres by lorry, train or ship, a process that uses fuel and sometimes causes the produce to lose its freshness. In response, a growing number of entrepreneurs and city planners are asking an unusual question: could we grow food in the city itself?
paras.B: The answer, increasingly, is yes. Urban farms already exist on the roofs of supermarkets, in disused car parks and even in underground tunnels. One of the most popular methods is hydroponics, in which plants grow in water enriched with nutrients instead of soil. Because the roots receive exactly what they need, the plants develop quickly, and a hydroponic farm can use up to ninety per cent less water than an ordinary field. Another method, vertical farming, stacks trays of plants on shelves, one above another, in a building. Special lamps replace sunlight, and computers control the temperature and humidity.
paras.C: The benefits are considerable. Lettuce, herbs and tomatoes grown a few kilometres from the customer arrive within hours of picking, so they taste better and contain more vitamins. Fewer lorries on the road mean lower emissions. Since the plants are grown indoors, farmers do not need pesticides, and bad weather cannot destroy the crop. Urban farms also create jobs in the city, and they can bring a sense of community: in several neighbourhoods, residents help to grow vegetables on shared rooftops and then take them home.
paras.D: Nevertheless, critics point out some serious difficulties. The lamps and machines used in vertical farms consume large amounts of electricity, and unless this comes from renewable sources, the environmental advantage disappears. The cost of setting up a modern indoor farm is also high, and many companies have closed because they could not sell their produce at a profitable price. At present, most urban farms grow leafy vegetables and herbs, which are light and quick to grow. Staple crops such as wheat and rice require far more space and energy and are unlikely to be grown in this way in the near future.
paras.E: For these reasons, experts do not expect urban farming to replace traditional agriculture. They see it as a useful addition, particularly for crops that spoil quickly and for cities that are far from farmland. Some researchers also believe that the greatest value may be educational: children who plant seeds on a school roof learn where their food comes from, and that knowledge may change the way they eat for the rest of their lives.
paras.F: There are also lessons for developing countries. In crowded cities in Africa and South Asia, small plots on rooftops and balconies already supply families with fresh vegetables, and simple low-cost systems using recycled containers have proved effective. These projects need little money and no advanced technology, yet they improve nutrition and provide a small income. Aid organisations now encourage them, arguing that the future of urban food may lie as much in modest local initiatives as in high-technology towers.

paras.A: Walk into any shop, hospital or school and you will notice that colour has been chosen with care. Fast-food restaurants favour red and yellow; banks prefer blue; hospitals use soft greens and whites. Designers believe that colour influences how we feel and behave, and a whole industry is built on this idea. But how much of it is true, and how much is simply tradition?
paras.B: Some effects have been tested in experiments. In one well-known study, students who saw a red cover on an exam paper before taking a test performed slightly worse than those who saw a green or grey cover. The researchers suggested that red is associated with danger and failure, because teachers use it to mark errors. Other studies show that people in a room with warm light tend to feel more comfortable and sociable than in a room lit by cool, bluish light.
paras.C: Many associations, however, depend on culture. In most Western countries, white is the colour of weddings and purity, while in parts of Asia, it is traditionally worn at funerals. Red means luck and celebration in China, but in some African countries, it is linked with mourning. Even within a single society, the meaning can change with time: pink was once considered a strong colour for boys, and blue a delicate colour for girls, the opposite of today's custom.
paras.D: Marketing specialists use colour because it works quickly. People form an opinion about a product in a few seconds, and research indicates that colour accounts for much of that first impression. A company that wants to seem trustworthy may use blue, while one that wishes to appear natural and healthy may choose green. At the same time, the effect should not be exaggerated. A bad product in an attractive package will not sell for long.
paras.E: The wise conclusion, many psychologists argue, is that colour affects us, but gently. It can support a mood, but it cannot create one. A bright classroom may help children to stay alert, but it cannot make a boring lesson exciting. Therefore, those who design our environments should treat colour as one tool among many, and they should remember that the people who look at it bring their own experiences, memories and cultures with them.
paras.F: It is also worth remembering that people differ. Some individuals are colour-blind and cannot distinguish certain shades, and others simply dislike a colour for personal reasons, perhaps because it reminds them of a place or a person. A designer who ignores such differences risks creating a space that works for the average person but for nobody in particular. The best advice may be to test ideas with real users before painting the walls.

paras.A: More than seventy per cent of our planet is covered by water, yet we have explored only a tiny part of it. The deepest regions of the ocean, which lie several kilometres beneath the surface, are dark, cold and under enormous pressure. At the bottom of the deepest trench, the water pushes down on every surface with a force roughly a thousand times greater than at sea level. For centuries, scientists believed that nothing could live in such conditions.
paras.B: They were wrong. In the 1970s, a small submarine descended to a crack in the sea floor and found hot springs rising from the rock. Around them, thousands of living creatures were gathered: giant worms, shrimps and pale crabs. These animals did not depend on sunlight, which never reaches such depths. Instead, they relied on bacteria that convert chemicals from the hot water into energy. The discovery showed that life can exist without the sun, and it changed the way scientists think about the origins of life.
paras.C: Exploring the deep sea is extremely difficult. Human divers cannot go below a few hundred metres, so researchers use submarines and remotely operated vehicles. These machines carry lights, cameras and mechanical arms, and they are controlled from a ship on the surface by cable. Each journey is expensive, and a single mission can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Some of the most interesting animals are also fragile: when brought to the surface, many of them die because of the change in pressure.
paras.D: Yet the rewards are high. Scientists have found hundreds of new species, many with strange adaptations. Some fish produce their own light to attract prey; others have enormous mouths so that they can swallow food larger than themselves in a place where meals are rare. Some of the chemicals extracted from deep-sea creatures are being tested as possible medicines for cancer and infections.
paras.E: The ocean floor also contains valuable minerals, such as copper and cobalt, and some companies would like to mine them. Environmental groups warn that mining could destroy habitats that may take thousands of years to recover, and they argue that we should learn more before we start. The debate shows a typical dilemma of science: the more we explore, the more we discover that there is to protect, and the more we realise how little we know.
paras.F: Technology is making exploration easier. New robots can stay underwater for months, collecting data automatically and sending it to scientists on shore. Cameras are becoming smaller and more sensitive, and sound waves are used to draw detailed maps of the sea floor. Within a few decades, researchers hope to map the whole ocean in the same detail as the surface of the Moon. Considering that we already have better maps of Mars than of our own seabed, this would be a notable achievement.

paras.A: Memory seems simple: we experience something, store it and later retrieve it. In reality, it is a complex process involving several systems in the brain. Psychologists often divide memory into three stages. The first, sensory memory, holds a brief impression of what we see or hear for only a second or two. Information that receives attention then moves into short-term memory, where it stays for about twenty seconds unless it is repeated. Only a small part of it reaches the third stage, long-term memory, where it can last for years.
paras.B: A famous experiment showed how limited short-term memory is. People can usually hold about seven items, such as digits in a telephone number, at one time. This is why long numbers are divided into groups: five or six small groups are easier to remember than one long string. Researchers call this technique 'chunking', and memory champions use it to recall hundreds of digits.
paras.C: Long-term memory is divided into different types. Some memories concern events and facts, such as the capital of a country or the day of your birthday party. Others involve skills, such as riding a bicycle or tying a shoelace, which we perform automatically without recalling how we learned them. The second type is particularly durable. A person may not ride a bicycle for twenty years and still manage after a few wobbly metres.
paras.D: Contrary to what many people believe, memory is not like a video recording. Each time we recall an event, we rebuild it from pieces, and this process can introduce mistakes. Witnesses to a crime, for example, may be absolutely sure about details that turn out to be false, and their confidence does not guarantee accuracy. Experiments have shown that even a small suggestion in a question, such as 'How fast was the car going when it smashed into the other?', can change what people remember.
paras.E: Fortunately, there are ways to improve memory. Sleep helps the brain to store new information, so a good night's rest is more useful than an extra hour of late-night study. Spreading study over several days is more effective than learning everything at once, and explaining a topic to another person forces the brain to organise it. Exercise and a healthy diet also play a role. In short, memory is not a fixed gift but a skill that can be developed.
paras.F: Finally, memory changes with age, but not always for the worse. Older people may take longer to recall names, yet they often have richer knowledge and better judgement. Studies suggest that people who keep learning new things, such as a language or a musical instrument, maintain their mental abilities longer. The brain, like a muscle, appears to benefit from regular challenge, and it is never too late to begin.

title: The Rise of the Electric Car

paras.A: The electric car is not a new invention. In the early 1900s, battery-powered cars were quiet, clean and easy to start, and they were popular in cities. But petrol cars soon took over. Oil was cheap, petrol engines allowed longer journeys, and the invention of the electric starter removed the need for a hard hand crank. For almost a hundred years, electric vehicles were rare curiosities.
paras.B: Concern about air pollution and the climate has brought them back. Cars with petrol or diesel engines release exhaust gases which damage health, especially in crowded cities, and contribute to global warming. An electric motor produces no fumes from the vehicle itself. It is also remarkably efficient: it converts most of the energy from its battery into movement, whereas a petrol engine wastes much of its fuel as heat.
paras.C: Governments have supported the change with money and rules. Many countries offer tax reductions or direct payments to people who buy electric cars, and several have announced that sales of new petrol cars will be banned within the next twenty years. At the same time, manufacturers are investing billions in new models, and the choice available to customers is expanding rapidly.
paras.D: However, there are obstacles. Batteries are expensive, and a car may cost more than a similar petrol model. Drivers worry about range, since the distance a car can travel on a single charge is shorter than that of a full petrol tank, and charging takes longer than filling up. In areas with few charging stations, longer trips can be difficult to plan. Another question concerns the electricity itself. If it comes from coal power stations, the environmental benefit is reduced, although studies suggest that electric cars still produce fewer emissions over their lifetime.
paras.E: The future depends on several factors: how quickly batteries become cheaper and lighter, how fast charging networks grow and how clean the electricity supply becomes. Experts expect that, within a decade, electric cars will cost no more than petrol cars in many markets. For city dwellers, who drive short distances and can charge at home, the change may come even sooner. The quiet hum of the electric car, once a curiosity, may soon be the normal sound of the street.
paras.F: Public transport is likely to change as well. Several cities have replaced diesel buses with electric ones, and the results have been encouraging: quieter streets, cleaner air and lower running costs. Delivery companies are testing electric vans for city routes, where the distances are short and the vehicles return to the same depot every night. If these experiments succeed, the effect on urban air quality could be much greater than that of private cars alone.

paras.A: Twenty years ago, most people kept in touch by telephone, letter or face-to-face meetings. Today, billions of people use websites and apps that let them share photographs, opinions and messages with friends and strangers. These platforms, known as social media, have changed the way we communicate, shop, learn and even think about ourselves.
paras.B: The benefits are real. Families separated by thousands of kilometres can talk to each other for free, and groups of people who share a rare hobby or illness can find one another. Small businesses use social media to advertise cheaply, and during disasters, messages posted online have helped rescuers to find people in need. News can also travel around the world within minutes.
paras.C: However, there are also concerns. Many apps are designed to hold attention, using features such as endless scrolling and notifications that bring users back again and again. Some researchers link heavy use with poor sleep and anxiety, especially among teenagers, though others point out that the evidence is mixed and that the effects depend on how people use the apps.
paras.D: Another problem is false information. A shocking rumour usually spreads faster than a careful correction, because people share what surprises or angers them without checking it first. Companies have tried to label false posts and to remove the most harmful, but critics say they act too slowly, while others warn that removing posts may limit free speech.
paras.E: There are also questions about privacy. Platforms collect large amounts of information about their users, such as the pages they visit and the friends they have, and use it to show advertisements that are likely to interest them. Most users agree to this without reading the long terms and conditions, and many are unaware of how much they are sharing.
paras.F: Experts therefore advise a balanced approach. Users can turn off unnecessary notifications, set limits on the time they spend online and think before they share. Schools increasingly teach 'digital literacy', which helps young people to judge sources and protect their personal details. Social media is a tool, and like any tool, its value depends on the way it is used. Parents and teachers can help by talking openly with children about what they see online, rather than simply forbidding it, so that young users learn to ask for help when something goes wrong.

paras.A: There are about seven thousand languages in the world today, but linguists estimate that nearly half of them may disappear by the end of this century. On average, one language dies every few weeks. When the last speaker of a language passes away, an entire way of describing the world goes with him, along with songs, stories and knowledge that were never written down.
paras.B: Why do languages die? The most common reason is not violence or ban, but a gradual change of habit. Parents decide that their children will have better opportunities if they speak a dominant language such as English, Russian or Chinese, so they stop using the local language at home. Within two generations, the children can understand their grandparents but no longer reply. Urbanisation speeds up the process, because young people who move to cities live among speakers of other languages.
paras.C: The loss is more than sentimental. Small languages often contain detailed knowledge of the environment. Some communities have dozens of words for types of snow, plants or weather, and many of these plants have medical uses that science has not yet studied. Languages also shape the way people think about time, family and colour. Linguists regard each of them as a unique experiment in human communication, and when one disappears, an experiment ends for ever.
paras.D: Yet there are reasons for hope. In New Zealand, the Maori language was nearly lost in the middle of the twentieth century, but a movement started 'language nests', pre-schools where children hear only Maori. Today, the language has official status and is taught in many schools. Similarly, Welsh, which once seemed to be in decline, is now spoken by about a quarter of the people in Wales, partly because it is used in road signs, television and education.
paras.E: Technology can also help. Researchers record elderly speakers and create dictionaries that can be studied online. Smartphone applications now teach languages with only a few thousand speakers, and social media allows scattered communities to talk to each other in their own tongue. In some cases, young people have found that writing messages in a heritage language is fashionable rather than old-fashioned.
paras.F: Nevertheless, experts stress that revival requires more than enthusiasm. A language survives only if people use it in daily life: at home, at work and in public places. Governments can help by supporting schools and media, but the decisive step is taken by families. As one linguist puts it, 'A language does not live in a dictionary. It lives in the kitchen.'

paras.A: Today, we pay for goods with banknotes, cards and phones, and we rarely think about what money really is. Yet for most of history, people lived without it. In the earliest societies, individuals traded directly, exchanging a sheep for a bag of grain or a pot for a knife. This system, called barter, works only if each person happens to want what the other has, and finding such a match could take a long time.
paras.B: To solve the problem, communities began to use objects that everybody accepted as payment. In different places, these included shells, salt, cattle and beads. The ideal 'money' needed to be durable, portable, divisible and hard to copy. Metals, especially gold and silver, fulfilled these conditions well, and by about 2,700 years ago, the first metal coins appeared in the kingdom of Lydia, in present-day Turkey. Each coin carried a stamp to show its weight and value.
paras.C: China introduced another invention. As trade increased, merchants found that carrying large quantities of heavy coins was inconvenient and dangerous. Around the year 1000, they began to deposit coins with trusted agents and take away paper receipts. The government soon recognised the advantage and issued official paper notes. When Marco Polo described the practice to Europeans, many found it difficult to believe that worthless paper could be exchanged for goods.
paras.D: In Europe, banks developed in the late Middle Ages. They kept valuables safe and made loans, and their notes were accepted as payment. For centuries, the value of paper money was linked to gold: in theory, anybody could exchange a note for a fixed amount of the metal. This link was gradually dropped in the twentieth century, and today the value of money depends on trust in the government that issues it.
paras.E: The most recent change is the move away from cash. In some countries, shops no longer accept coins or notes, and a payment can be made by simply touching a phone to a terminal. Digital money is fast and convenient, but critics worry about privacy and about people who have no bank accounts. Cryptocurrencies, which exist only on computers, add further uncertainty, and economists disagree about whether they will become real money or remain a fashion.
paras.F: What does the history of money teach us? Above all, that money is based on a shared belief. A piece of paper or a number on a screen has value only because people agree that it does. paras.A: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which hot rock, ash and gas escape from deep underground. There are about fifty to seventy eruptions each year, and roughly a tenth of the world's population lives within a hundred kilometres of an active volcano. Why would people choose to live in such a dangerous place? The answer lies in the soil.
paras.B: Volcanic ash contains many minerals, and over time it breaks down into extraordinarily fertile soil. Farmers on the slopes of volcanoes in Indonesia, Italy and Central America can harvest several crops a year, while neighbouring areas produce much less. In addition, volcanoes create valuable resources, such as hot water for heating, minerals for industry and spectacular scenery that attracts tourists. For many families, the benefits outweigh the risks, at least in ordinary times.
paras.C: The risks, however, are real. A violent eruption can throw ash high into the air, and the weight of ash on roofs may cause houses to collapse. Even more dangerous are pyroclastic flows, fast-moving clouds of hot gas and rock that can travel faster than a car and destroy everything in their path. In 79 AD, such a flow buried the Roman town of Pompeii within hours, preserving buildings and objects that archaeologists still study today.
paras.D: Fortunately, scientists can now predict many eruptions. Instruments on the slopes measure small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground and the gases released from vents. When these signs become stronger, experts warn the authorities, who can order an evacuation. In 1991, such a warning in the Philippines saved tens of thousands of lives before a huge eruption of Mount Pinatubo. Nevertheless, predictions are never perfect, and a volcano may remain quiet for centuries before suddenly waking up.
paras.E: Eruptions can affect the whole planet. The same Pinatubo eruption sent so much gas into the atmosphere that global temperatures fell by about half a degree for the next two years. In 1815, the eruption of Mount Tambora was followed by a year without a proper summer in Europe and North America, with failed harvests and widespread hunger. Scientists study these events to understand how the climate responds to sudden changes.
paras.F: Communities near volcanoes therefore live with both opportunity and uncertainty. They practise evacuations, build shelters and learn to recognise the warning signs. Many have a close relationship with the mountain and treat it with respect rather than fear. As one farmer on the slopes of Mount Etna said, 'The mountain gives us our bread, and sometimes it asks for something in return.'

paras.A: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand. A monk might spend a year producing a single Bible, and because each copy was so expensive, only churches, universities and the very rich could afford one. Most people never owned a book, and many could not read at all. Knowledge was a scarce resource, controlled by a small group.
paras.B: The situation changed around 1450, when a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg developed a system of printing with movable metal letters. The idea of printing was not new: the Chinese and Koreans had used wooden blocks and even movable type centuries earlier. But Gutenberg combined several inventions: a durable metal alloy for the letters, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal and a press adapted from the machines used to crush grapes. The combination allowed him to produce many identical pages quickly.
paras.C: The effect was dramatic. Within fifty years, printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred European cities, and millions of books had been produced. Prices fell sharply, and ordinary merchants and craftsmen began to build small libraries. Scholars in different countries could read the same texts, and they discovered each other's errors much faster than before. Many historians connect the spread of printing with the rapid growth of science in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
paras.D: Printing also changed religion and politics. When the reformer Martin Luther criticised the Church in 1517, his ideas were printed and spread across Germany within weeks. Rulers and church leaders realised the power of the new technology and tried to control it by censoring books and punishing printers. These efforts were rarely successful, because it was easy to print a pamphlet in secret and carry it from one town to another.
paras.E: Languages were affected as well. Printers needed to decide which spelling and grammar to use, and their choices helped to standardise national languages. As more people learned to read in their own tongue, rather than in Latin, local literature flourished. The first novels, newspapers and school textbooks appeared in this period, and a reading public began to take shape.
paras.F: Some people see a parallel with the internet today. Both technologies reduced the cost of sharing information and enabled ideas to spread without permission. Both brought great benefits and new problems, among them the circulation of false information. The history of printing suggests that societies take time to learn how to use a new medium wisely, and that the learning is rarely smooth.

paras.A: Water covers most of the planet, but only about three per cent of it is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers or hidden deep underground. The water that people can easily reach in rivers, lakes and shallow wells is less than one per cent of the total. As the population grows and cities expand, this small amount is under increasing pressure.
paras.B: Experts say that more than two billion people live in countries where the supply of water is seriously inadequate. In some regions, women and children walk several hours a day to collect water, which prevents girls from attending school. Even when water is available, it is often unsafe. Dirty drinking water spreads diseases such as cholera and typhoid, and these illnesses kill hundreds of thousands of people every year.
paras.C: Agriculture is the largest user of fresh water, accounting for about seventy per cent of the total taken from rivers and wells. Much of it is wasted. Traditional irrigation, in which fields are flooded, loses large quantities to evaporation and leaks. In Central Asia, the diversion of rivers to grow cotton led to the shrinking of the Aral Sea, one of the worst environmental disasters of the last century.
paras.D: Climate change is making matters worse. Glaciers in mountain ranges such as the Himalayas and the Tien Shan act as natural reservoirs, releasing meltwater to rivers in the dry summer months. As they shrink, the flow may increase for a while, but in the long run, there will be less water. Rainfall patterns are also changing, with some regions suffering longer droughts and others facing more violent floods.
paras.E: Fortunately, there are practical solutions. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots of plants and can reduce consumption by half. Cities can repair leaking pipes, which in some places lose a third of the water that passes through them. Wastewater can be cleaned and used again for factories or gardens, and in countries with a coast, desalination plants turn seawater into drinking water, although this process is expensive and uses a lot of energy.
paras.F: Individuals can also make a difference. Closing a tap while brushing teeth, repairing a dripping tap and choosing foods that require less water are small steps that add up when millions of people take them. paras.A: Since the launch of the first satellite in 1957, humans have sent thousands of objects into orbit. Many of them have stopped working, but they have not disappeared. Dead satellites, rocket parts and fragments of metal continue to circle the Earth at speeds of up to eight kilometres a second. Together, they form a cloud of 'space debris' that scientists regard as an increasing danger.
paras.B: Size is not the main issue. Even a piece of paint smaller than a coin, travelling at such speed, can damage a spacecraft's window. Larger objects can destroy a satellite completely. The International Space Station has had to change its orbit several times to avoid a collision, and astronauts occasionally take shelter in an escape capsule when a piece of debris approaches too close.
paras.C: The problem is growing because collisions create more debris. In 2009, an American communications satellite and a Russian military satellite collided and broke into thousands of fragments. Two years earlier, in 2007, a country tested a missile against its own old satellite and increased the number of dangerous pieces by about a quarter. Scientists warn of a possible chain reaction, known as the Kessler syndrome, in which each collision produces fragments that cause further collisions until certain orbits are unusable.
paras.D: Why does this matter to ordinary people? Satellites supply weather forecasts, telephone and internet connections, navigation and television signals. Farmers use satellite data to decide when to plant seeds; ships and aeroplanes use it to find their way. If a key orbit became unusable, the consequences for the economy and safety would be serious.
paras.E: Solutions are being developed. New satellites are designed to return to the atmosphere and burn up at the end of their lives, so that they do not remain in orbit. Several companies are testing machines that can capture old satellites with nets, harpoons or robotic arms and pull them down. Others suggest using lasers to push small fragments into lower orbits where the atmosphere would destroy them.
paras.F: All these ideas require international cooperation, because space belongs to nobody and everybody. Agreements on rules already exist, but enforcing them is difficult, and the number of satellites is increasing every year as private companies launch large networks. title: Coral Reefs: Cities of the Sea

paras.A: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. This extraordinary variety has earned them the name 'rainforests of the sea'. Fish, turtles, sharks, crabs and thousands of other creatures find food and shelter among the corals, and the reefs also protect coasts from storms by absorbing the energy of waves.
paras.B: Corals themselves are animals, although they look like plants or rocks. Each coral is formed of many tiny creatures called polyps, which build a hard skeleton of limestone around themselves. Inside their bodies live microscopic algae that supply them with food through photosynthesis, and in return, the polyps provide a home. This partnership explains why reefs grow only in clear, shallow, sunlit water in warm seas, and why they develop very slowly: a large reef may take thousands of years to form.
paras.C: Today, reefs are in serious danger. One of the main threats is a rise in ocean temperature. When the water becomes too hot, the corals expel the algae that live in them, turn white and may die. This process, called bleaching, has affected reefs in every ocean, and the Great Barrier Reef in Australia has suffered several severe episodes in recent decades. Another threat is acidification: the sea absorbs part of the carbon dioxide released by human activities, and this makes the water more acidic and weakens the skeletons of the corals.
paras.D: Local pressures add to the problem. Fertilisers and sewage that flow from the land into the sea feed algae that cover the corals and block the light. In some places, fishermen use explosives or poison, which destroy large areas in minutes. Careless tourists who touch or break corals, or anchor their boats on reefs, also cause damage.
paras.E: The economic effects are considerable. Hundreds of millions of people depend on reefs for food and income from fishing and tourism. If the reefs disappeared, many coastal communities would lose both their livelihood and their natural protection against storms. Scientists estimate that the value of services provided by reefs amounts to billions of dollars a year.
paras.F: There is hope, however. Marine reserves, in which fishing is restricted, have allowed damaged reefs to recover. Scientists are growing heat-resistant corals in laboratories and planting them on damaged reefs. These efforts will not save the reefs unless the underlying causes are tackled, but they give time. The most important step, researchers say, is to reduce the emissions that warm and acidify the sea.

title: Marie Curie: A Life in Science

paras.A: Maria Sklodowska was born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when Poland was under foreign rule and women were not allowed to study at university. Despite her outstanding talent, she had to work as a governess to pay for her sister's studies in Paris, and only at the age of twenty-four did she enter the Sorbonne, the famous French university. She lived in a tiny room, often with little food, and studied physics and mathematics with such dedication that she finished at the top of her class.
paras.B: In Paris, she met Pierre Curie, a physicist, and they married in 1895. Together they began to investigate a mysterious form of energy discovered by Henri Becquerel in uranium. Marie coined the term 'radioactivity' to describe it. Working in a leaky shed that had once been used for storing potatoes, the couple processed tonnes of ore by hand to isolate tiny amounts of two new elements, which they named polonium, after her native country, and radium.
paras.C: In 1903, Marie, Pierre and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, making her the first woman to receive the award. Three years later, tragedy struck: Pierre was killed in a street accident. Marie was devastated, but she continued their work and took his position at the university, becoming the first woman to teach there. In 1911, she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, for the discovery of polonium and radium.
paras.D: When the First World War began, Marie recognised that X-rays could help surgeons to find bullets and broken bones. She designed mobile X-ray units, nicknamed 'little Curies', and trained women to operate them. By the end of the war, her vehicles and equipment had helped to examine over a million wounded soldiers. She even drove an ambulance herself.
paras.E: Her research had a cost. At that time, the dangers of radioactivity were poorly understood. Marie carried test tubes of radium in her pocket and kept them in her desk because she liked the pale blue glow they produced in the dark. Her notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead-lined boxes. She died in 1934 from an illness probably caused by long exposure to radiation.
paras.F: Marie Curie's influence reaches far beyond her discoveries. She showed that a woman could succeed in a field dominated by men, and she inspired generations of girls to study science. Radium and its descendants are used in the treatment of cancer, and the institute she founded in Paris is still a leading research centre. Her determination, curiosity and willingness to share knowledge remain a model for scientists everywhere.

paras.A: Chess is played by hundreds of millions of people, from children in school clubs to professionals who compete for large prizes. The game looks timeless, yet it has changed considerably over the centuries. Its ancestor, a game called chaturanga, appeared in India around the sixth century. paras.F: Research suggests that chess may benefit children. Studies in several countries found that pupils who learned the game improved their concentration and their ability to plan ahead. title: Tornadoes: Nature at its Most Violent

paras.A: A tornado is a rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground. It may be only a few metres wide or more than a kilometre, and the winds inside the strongest can exceed 450 kilometres an hour, faster than any other wind on Earth. Tornadoes occur on every continent except Antarctica, but nowhere are they more common than in the central United States, in an area known as 'Tornado Alley'.
paras.B: The conditions that create a tornado are well understood in general terms, though not in every detail. Warm, damp air near the ground meets cooler, dry air above. As the warm air rises, it forms a towering storm cloud, and if winds at different heights move in different directions, the rising air starts to spin. In some cases, this rotation tightens and stretches downward until it touches the ground. Many storms show signs of rotation, but only a small proportion produce a tornado, and this is one reason why forecasting is so difficult.
paras.C: The Fujita scale measures the strength of tornadoes according to the damage they cause. The weakest, rated zero, break branches and damage signs. The strongest, rated five, can lift well-built houses from their foundations and carry cars for hundreds of metres. Fortunately, about three-quarters of tornadoes are weak, and the strongest account for around one per cent, though they cause most of the deaths.
paras.D: Warning systems have saved many lives. Radar can detect rotation inside storms, and meteorologists issue alerts when a tornado is likely. Today, the average warning time is about ten minutes, which is enough for people to move to a basement or a small room without windows near the centre of the building. Mobile homes and cars offer little protection, and experts advise people in them to go to a strong shelter if possible.
paras.E: Research is attempting to improve forecasts. Teams of scientists, known as storm chasers, drive towards storms carrying instruments, and aircraft fly above clouds to measure temperature and moisture. Computer models now simulate the formation of tornadoes in great detail. The aim is to increase warning times to half an hour or more, and to reduce false alarms, which tend to make people ignore later warnings.
paras.F: Some people connect tornadoes with climate change, but the evidence is not conclusive. Records are incomplete, especially for the past, because tornadoes in unpopulated areas often went unreported. What scientists do agree on is that the number of people living in the path of storms is increasing, so even if tornadoes themselves do not change, the potential damage may.

paras.A: For most of history, doctors could learn about the inside of the human body only by cutting it open. The discovery of X-rays in 1895 changed everything. A German physicist, Wilhelm Röntgen, was experimenting with electric tubes when he noticed that a screen coated with special chemicals glowed in a dark room, although the tube was covered. He realised that an invisible ray was passing through the cover. Within weeks, he had produced a photograph of the bones in his wife's hand, complete with her wedding ring.
paras.B: The news spread quickly, and within a year, doctors in several countries were using X-rays to find broken bones and swallowed objects. The technique soon became standard in hospitals. However, the dangers of radiation were not understood, and many early users developed serious burns. Safety rules, including lead aprons and limits on exposure, were introduced only gradually, and today, the dose from a single X-ray is very small.
paras.C: In the 1970s, a new technology called CT, or computed tomography, was developed. A CT scanner takes many X-ray pictures from different angles as it rotates around the patient, and a computer combines them into detailed images of slices through the body. For the first time, doctors could see soft organs such as the brain, liver and kidneys without surgery. The inventors received the Nobel Prize in 1979, and CT scans are now used for diagnosing tumours, bleeding and injuries.
paras.D: Another method, magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses no X-rays at all. The patient lies inside a large tube containing a powerful magnet, and radio waves cause the hydrogen atoms in the body to send out signals. A computer converts these signals into pictures. MRI produces especially clear images of soft tissue such as muscles, joints and the brain, and it does not involve any radiation, which makes it safer for repeated use. However, the machine is noisy, expensive and unsuitable for people with certain metal implants.
paras.E: Ultrasound, which uses high-frequency sound waves, is perhaps the most familiar technique, because it is used to show unborn babies. A small device is moved over the skin, and the echoes of sound waves are turned into a moving picture. It is cheap, painless and portable, and it can be carried to remote villages.
paras.F: Medical imaging continues to develop. Artificial intelligence programmes are being trained to examine thousands of pictures and recognise early signs of disease, sometimes more accurately than doctors. Experts believe that the best results will come from cooperation: the computer detects patterns, and the doctor decides what they mean.

paras.A: Smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases in history. For thousands of years, it killed up to a third of those who caught it and left survivors with deep scars on their faces. In the eighteenth century alone, it caused hundreds of millions of deaths worldwide. Kings and peasants were equally at risk, and nobody knew how to stop it.
paras.B: Some societies, however, had noticed that people who survived the disease never caught it again. In parts of Asia and Africa, healers deliberately gave healthy people a small amount of material from a smallpox sore, hoping to cause a mild illness. This practice, called variolation, often worked, but it was risky: some patients developed the full disease and died, and they could also infect others.
paras.C: The breakthrough came in 1796 from an English country doctor, Edward Jenner. He had heard a local belief that milkmaids, who often caught a mild illness called cowpox from cattle, did not get smallpox. Jenner decided to test the idea. He took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and injected it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. The boy suffered a mild fever. Weeks later, Jenner exposed him to smallpox, and the boy stayed healthy.
paras.D: Jenner called his method 'vaccination', from the Latin word for cow, vacca. Today, such an experiment on a child would be considered unethical, but the result was clear. Despite opposition from some doctors and religious groups, who thought it unnatural, the method spread across Europe and beyond. Within a few years, governments began to organise vaccination programmes, and in some countries, it became compulsory.
paras.E: In the twentieth century, the World Health Organization launched an ambitious plan to wipe out the disease. Teams travelled to remote villages, found cases and vaccinated everyone around them, a strategy known as 'ring vaccination'. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980, the organisation declared that smallpox had been eradicated. It remains the only human disease to have been completely removed in this way.
paras.F: The story has lasting lessons. It shows how careful observation can lead to discoveries, and how international cooperation can solve problems that no country could solve alone. Many scientists hope that the same approach will one day succeed against other diseases, such as polio, which is now close to disappearing.

paras.A: In the third century BC, the Egyptian city of Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great, was one of the largest and richest in the world. Its rulers, the Ptolemies, wanted it to be a centre of culture as well as trade. They founded a great institution known as the Museum, a place of research and teaching, and next to it, they built the most famous library of the ancient world.
paras.B: The aim of the library was ambitious: to collect all the books in the known world. Agents were sent to buy scrolls in other countries, and ships arriving in the port were searched. If a ship carried books, the scrolls were taken to the library and copied. The owners received the copies, while the originals stayed in Alexandria. According to some sources, the collection grew to several hundred thousand scrolls, although modern historians believe that the true number was lower.
paras.C: The library attracted some of the greatest scholars of the age. Euclid is believed to have worked in Alexandria, collecting the knowledge of geometry in his famous book, the Elements. Eratosthenes, one of the chief librarians, measured the size of the Earth with surprising accuracy by comparing the length of shadows in two cities at the same time of day. Others studied medicine, astronomy and literature, and they compared and corrected the texts of poets such as Homer.
paras.D: What happened to the library? Many people imagine that it was destroyed in a single fire, but the reality is probably more complicated. Julius Caesar's soldiers set fire to ships in the harbour in 48 BC, and the flames may have damaged part of the collection. Later, the city suffered from wars, and the support of the rulers declined. Scholars left, funds ran out and the library slowly lost its importance. By the fourth century AD, little remained.
paras.E: The loss was great, because many works survived only in a few copies. Of the plays of the Greek writers, for example, only a small fraction has reached us. Yet the library's real legacy lies in the idea that knowledge should be gathered, preserved and shared. In 2002, a new library opened in Alexandria, close to the ancient site, as a tribute to the original. Its modern building is shaped like a giant sundial tilted towards the sea.
paras.F: The story of Alexandria carries a warning. Knowledge is fragile, and it depends on the support of societies. When wars, neglect or indifference weaken that support, the loss can be permanent. Today's digital archives may offer greater protection, but only if people continue to care for them.

paras.A: Music has been part of human life for at least forty thousand years. Archaeologists have found flutes made from bird bones and mammoth ivory in caves in Europe, and every known culture has songs, dances or instruments. Why did music become so universal? Scientists believe that the answer lies in the way it affects the brain.
paras.B: When a person listens to music, many parts of the brain work at once. Some areas process the sound itself, others handle rhythm and movement, and others deal with emotion and memory. This explains why a song can bring back a vivid memory of a particular place or person. Brain scans show that favourite pieces trigger the release of dopamine, a chemical connected with pleasure, in the same way as good food or a pleasant surprise.
paras.C: Learning to play an instrument has even stronger effects. Studies comparing children who take music lessons with those who do not have found that the first group tends to improve in memory and in the ability to hear differences between sounds. Musicians also show greater connection between the two halves of the brain. These benefits seem to be greater for those who start young, though adults who learn an instrument also gain some advantages.
paras.D: Music can also help people who are ill. Doctors use it to reduce pain and anxiety before operations, and patients with certain brain injuries have recovered speech by singing words that they could not say. In people suffering from dementia, familiar songs can wake memories that seemed lost; relatives report that a person who rarely speaks may suddenly sing every word of a childhood song.
paras.E: A popular idea claims that listening to classical music makes children more intelligent. This is known as the 'Mozart effect', and it originated from a small study in 1993, which found a short-term improvement in a spatial test after listening to a piece by Mozart. Later research failed to confirm that the music made people cleverer. The improvement, if there was one, probably came from a better mood or alertness, and it disappeared quickly.
paras.F: What is certain is that music brings people together. Singing in a choir, dancing at a wedding or clapping at a concert creates a feeling of belonging. Experiments show that people who sing together even synchronise their heartbeats. Perhaps this, rather than any effect on intelligence, is the real reason why music has been with us for so long.

paras.A: At the beginning of the twentieth century, much of Antarctica was unexplored, and the South Pole had never been reached. The continent is the coldest, windiest and driest on Earth. Temperatures can fall below minus sixty degrees, and the ice sheet is up to four kilometres thick. Nevertheless, two expeditions set out in 1910 with the same goal, and their story has become one of the most famous in the history of exploration.
paras.B: The first was led by the Norwegian Roald Amundsen, who had experience of polar conditions. He planned with great care. His team used dogs to pull sledges, wore clothes of animal skins like those of the local Arctic peoples, and laid food stores along the route. When the dogs became tired, some were killed to feed the others, a hard decision but a practical one. On 14 December 1911, Amundsen and four companions reached the Pole.
paras.C: The second expedition was led by the British naval officer Robert Falcon Scott. Scott's team also hoped to reach the Pole first, but his preparations were less well suited to the environment. He relied on motor sledges, which broke down in the cold, and on ponies, which suffered terribly in the snow. In the end, the men themselves had to pull the heavy sledges. Scott's party reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, only to find a Norwegian tent and flag already there.
paras.D: The return journey ended in tragedy. The weather turned unusually cold, and the men were weakened by hunger and frostbite. One member died after a fall, another walked out of the tent into a blizzard in the hope of saving his friends. Scott and his two remaining companions were trapped by a storm only eighteen kilometres from a food store. Their bodies were found eight months later, together with diaries that described their last days with extraordinary calm.
paras.E: Why did one expedition succeed and the other fail? Historians stress several reasons: Amundsen chose better methods, had a smaller and more experienced team and focused on a single goal. Scott, on the other hand, also wanted to carry out scientific work, and his men carried heavy rock samples to the end. Bad luck contributed, but experts agree that good planning would probably have prevented disaster.
paras.F: Today, Antarctica is governed by an international treaty that bans military activities and protects the environment. Hundreds of scientists work there each summer, studying ice, climate and wildlife. Visitors arriving by ship are reminded of the lesson of 1912: in extreme places, respect, preparation and humility are more valuable than courage alone.

paras.A: Look up on a clear night far from any city, and you may see thousands of stars, the pale band of the Milky Way and perhaps even a shooting star. In most places today, however, this sight has vanished. Streetlights, advertisements and brightly lit buildings create a glow that hides all but the brightest stars. Astronomers call this 'light pollution', and it is increasing by several per cent every year.
paras.B: For centuries, people watched the sky to find their way, to plan the seasons and to understand their place in the universe. Many cultures developed stories about the constellations, and many scientific discoveries began with observation. A child growing up in a modern city may never see the Milky Way. In a survey, a large proportion of urban teenagers could not name a single constellation, and some did not know that the Moon changes its shape.
paras.C: Artificial light is not just a problem for astronomers. Many animals depend on darkness. Sea turtles hatch on beaches at night and move towards the brightest horizon, which is normally the sea. Near hotels and lights, the baby turtles go the wrong way and die. Migrating birds are confused by lit towers and collide with buildings. Insects circle lamps until they are exhausted, and since insects are food for many animals, the effects spread through the food chain.
paras.D: Humans are affected, too. Our bodies follow a daily rhythm controlled partly by light, and exposure to bright light at night can disturb the production of a hormone that helps us to sleep. Research has linked night-time light to sleeping difficulties and, in some studies, to a higher risk of certain illnesses, although more work is needed to establish the connection firmly.
paras.E: The good news is that light pollution is one of the easiest forms of pollution to reduce. Lamps can be shielded so that light shines downwards, not into the sky, and they can be fitted with warmer colours, which are less harmful. Lights can be switched off or dimmed when nobody needs them. These measures usually save electricity as well, and several cities that adopted them have reported lower bills.
paras.F: Some places have gone further and created 'dark sky reserves', areas where lighting is strictly controlled. They attract astronomers and tourists, and local people often take pride in the stars above them. The idea is simple: a clear night sky belongs to everybody, and protecting it costs less than losing it.

paras.A: Along tropical coasts, there are trees that grow with their roots in salt water. These are mangroves, and the dense forests they form are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth. At first glance, they look muddy and uninviting, but beneath the surface, they are full of life. Mangroves are found in more than a hundred countries, from Indonesia and Brazil to Nigeria and Pakistan.
paras.B: Survival in such conditions requires special adaptations. Ordinary trees die in salt water, but mangroves have developed ways to cope with it. Some filter salt through their roots, while others store it in leaves that eventually fall off, and a few push it out through glands. Because the mud lacks oxygen, many species grow aerial roots that rise above the water like straws and allow the tree to breathe. These tangled roots also hold the soil in place.
paras.C: The forests function as nurseries for the sea. Young fish, crabs and shrimps shelter among the roots, safe from larger predators, and when they grow, they swim out to open water. Scientists estimate that a high proportion of the fish caught in some tropical regions spend part of their lives in mangroves. Birds nest in the branches, and in some places, the forests also shelter monkeys, crocodiles and even tigers.
paras.D: Mangroves protect people as well. Their roots absorb the force of waves and reduce erosion, and they can lower the height of a storm surge. When a powerful tsunami struck the coast of Asia in 2004, villages behind dense mangroves generally suffered less damage than those on bare shores. Mangroves are also extremely good at storing carbon: they hold several times more carbon per hectare than most land forests, and much of it is locked in the mud for centuries.
paras.E: Despite these benefits, mangroves have disappeared at an alarming rate. Over the last fifty years, about a third of the world's mangrove forest has been lost. The main cause has been the creation of ponds for farming shrimp, which brings quick profits but ruins the soil within a few years. Other causes include building, pollution and cutting for firewood.
paras.F: There are signs of change. Many governments have banned the clearing of mangroves, and local communities in countries such as Vietnam and Kenya have planted millions of seedlings. Planting is not always successful, since seedlings placed in the wrong spot die, but projects that involve villagers and choose sites carefully achieve good results. As more people understand the value of these forests, the future looks a little brighter.

paras.A: Today we take zero for granted. It sits quietly in numbers like 10 and 100, and it is essential in mathematics, science and computing. Yet for thousands of years, nobody used it, and its arrival in the history of numbers was one of the most important intellectual events of all time. How did something that stands for nothing become so valuable?
paras.B: The earliest number systems had no symbol for zero. The Romans, for example, wrote numbers with letters, and did not need a sign for 'nothing' because they did not use place value. The Babylonians, who worked with a system based on sixty, left a space between digits to indicate an empty place, but this was confusing: two spaces could look like one. Later they introduced a mark to show a gap, though they did not treat it as a number that could be added or multiplied.
paras.C: The decisive step was taken in India. By the seventh century, Indian mathematicians such as Brahmagupta were using zero as a number in its own right and writing rules for it. They explained that adding zero changes nothing, and that multiplying any number by zero gives zero. Dividing by zero, however, caused difficulties that were not solved for centuries. The Indian system, with its ten digits, from zero to nine, and its use of place value, was more efficient than any earlier one.
paras.D: The knowledge travelled west. Scholars in Baghdad, including al-Khwarizmi, studied the Indian numbers and wrote about them in Arabic, and from the Islamic world, they entered Europe, partly through the book of Fibonacci, an Italian merchant who had learned them in North Africa. Many Europeans were suspicious. Some governments even banned the new numbers, claiming that zero made it easier to cheat, since a '0' could be changed to a '6' or a '9'. For a long time, merchants continued to keep their accounts in Roman numerals.
paras.E: Slowly, the advantages became undeniable. Calculation with Hindu-Arabic numerals was much quicker, and it made possible the growth of algebra, accounting and, eventually, the scientific revolution. Without zero, there would be no negative numbers, no decimals and no coordinates on a map. In the twentieth century, it formed the basis of binary code, in which zero and one are the only two digits, and every digital device depends on it.
paras.F: The story of zero is a reminder that the most useful ideas are not always obvious. It took centuries for humans to understand that a symbol for 'nothing' could have such power. Today, a schoolchild learns it in a few minutes, but behind this simple circle lies a long journey across cultures and continents.

paras.A: Many people believe that universities are a European invention of the Middle Ages, and the oldest degree-granting institutions in Europe, such as those of Bologna and Paris, date from the eleventh and twelfth centuries. But learning institutions existed in other parts of the world long before. In Fez, in present-day Morocco, a college founded in the ninth century by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri still operates, and in Cairo, al-Azhar was established in 970.
paras.B: In Central Asia, scholarship flourished in cities such as Bukhara, Samarkand and Khiva. Students attended madrasahs, where they studied the Quran, law and language, but also mathematics, astronomy and medicine. A scholar might travel hundreds of kilometres to listen to a famous teacher, and a diploma in the form of a certificate, written by the teacher, was a student's proof of knowledge. The reputation of the teacher, rather than the building, mattered most.
paras.C: In Europe, universities began as associations of students or teachers who joined together to protect their interests. The students of Bologna, for instance, hired professors and punished them if they did not give their lectures. Studies were divided into stages. A student first took a general course in grammar, logic and arithmetic, and only after that did he move to a higher faculty such as law, medicine or theology. Lectures were given in Latin, so that a student from England could study in Italy without difficulty.
paras.D: Life was not easy. Books were so expensive that most students had to listen carefully and write down what the professor read aloud. Rooms were cold, and discipline was strict: students could be fined for swearing or for carrying weapons. Quarrels between students and townspeople occasionally turned into riots. Yet the universities also had great freedoms. Their members were usually answerable to their own authorities, not to the local officials, and this independence protected scholars who held unusual ideas.
paras.E: Examinations were oral and public. A candidate had to defend his knowledge before a group of masters and answer difficult questions, and the ceremony might last for hours. Those who passed were given the right to teach, which is where the word 'master' and the modern degree 'master's' come from.
paras.F: The early universities left a lasting mark on education. They created traditions such as lectures, degrees and academic gowns, and they established the idea that knowledge should be debated openly. Despite changes in technology, many of these customs are still alive. A graduate in a cap and gown today follows, perhaps unwittingly, a path that thousands of students walked eight centuries ago.

paras.B: Why do companies use them? Robots do not get tired, bored or sick, and they can work in dangerous places: in extreme heat, among harmful chemicals or in tiny spaces. They also give consistent results. A robot arm that fixes a part to a car does so in exactly the same way ten thousand times. For many firms, the initial cost is high, but over a few years, the savings in wages, mistakes and accidents repay the investment.
paras.C: Not every robot looks like a human. Most are mechanical arms fixed to the floor, and others are wheeled machines that move goods around warehouses. Newer types, called 'collaborative robots', are designed to work beside people without safety fences. They have sensors that stop them when they touch something, and they can be taught by moving their arm by hand. A small workshop can use them for tasks such as lifting heavy boxes.
paras.D: The effect on employment is a subject of heated debate. Some studies suggest that robots have already replaced millions of jobs, especially routine tasks in manufacturing. Others point out that new technologies also create jobs: somebody must design, build, programme and repair the machines. Economists expect that the types of work will change rather than disappear, but the transition can be painful for people who lack the skills for the new positions.
paras.E: The key, many experts believe, is education. Workers whose jobs are at risk need opportunities to retrain, and schools need to teach skills that machines find difficult, such as creative thinking, communication and problem solving. Countries that invest in training are likely to benefit more from robots than those that do not.
paras.F: Looking ahead, robots are moving beyond factories. They clean floors, deliver meals in restaurants, assist surgeons and explore other planets. Yet engineers admit that machines are still poor at tasks that children find easy, like folding a shirt or understanding a joke. For the foreseeable future, humans and robots will probably work side by side, each doing what they do best.

paras.A: Tourism is one of the world's largest industries. Before the recent pandemic, more than one and a half billion international trips were made each year, and the sector supported roughly one job in ten. For many countries, especially small ones with few other resources, visitors bring money that pays for schools, roads and hospitals. A single hotel can employ hundreds of local people, from cooks and drivers to guides and cleaners.
paras.B: The benefits go beyond money. Tourism can encourage people to protect their heritage. Old buildings that might have been demolished are restored because visitors will pay to see them, and traditional crafts, music and dances find new audiences. paras.C: However, there are costs. Popular places can be overwhelmed. In the narrow streets of some historic cities, residents complain of crowds, noise and rising prices. Rents increase as flats are converted into holiday lets, and local families are pushed to the edges of town. Some cities have introduced limits on visitor numbers or taxes on overnight stays in an effort to restore balance. In Venice, for example, day visitors now pay an entry fee on busy days, and in Amsterdam, new hotels are restricted in the centre. Critics say these measures are unfair to ordinary travellers, but supporters argue that without them, the cities would lose the character that makes them worth visiting.
paras.D: Nature also suffers. Walkers wear away paths, boats damage coral reefs and aeroplanes release large amounts of carbon dioxide. A holiday involving a long flight can produce more emissions than months of ordinary living. Hotels in dry regions may use enormous amounts of water, leaving little for nearby villages. In some places, wildlife has been disturbed by visitors who come too close for photographs.
paras.E: In response, the idea of 'responsible tourism' has gained support. paras.A: Parents often wonder why teenagers behave as they do: sleeping late, taking risks, arguing and spending hours with friends. Until recently, many people blamed hormones. Now scientists believe that a large part of the explanation lies in the brain, which undergoes a remarkable reorganisation between the ages of about ten and twenty-five.
paras.B: One of the most important changes concerns the prefrontal cortex, the area at the front of the brain responsible for planning, decision-making and self-control. This region matures later than other parts, often not before the mid-twenties. Meanwhile, the areas that deal with emotion and reward develop earlier. The result is a brain that feels strongly and wants quick rewards but has not yet fully developed the brakes. This does not mean that teenagers are unable to think; it means that in situations of excitement or pressure from friends, their judgement may be less reliable.
paras.C: Experiments illustrate the point. In a driving simulation, teenagers took more risks when friends were watching than when they drove alone, whereas adults were not influenced. Brain scans showed that the reward centres of the teenagers became more active in the presence of friends. Researchers do not regard this as a defect; it may have helped young people in the past to leave the family and explore new places.
paras.D: The teenage years are also a period of rapid learning. The brain strengthens the connections that are used often and removes those that are not, a process sometimes described as 'use it or lose it'. A young person who practises a musical instrument, a sport or a language during this stage builds pathways that may last a lifetime. Because the brain is so adaptable, teenagers can learn new skills with remarkable speed, but they can also form unhelpful habits easily.
paras.E: What can adults do? Experts advise clear rules and calm discussion rather than constant criticism. Explaining the reasons behind a rule gives teenagers the chance to practise reasoning, and giving them responsibility in safe situations helps them to learn judgement. Sleep matters too, and as noted in other studies, teenagers need nine hours a night; those who sleep less find it harder to control their emotions.
paras.F: The key message is a hopeful one. A teenager's mind is not broken; it is under construction. With patience, support and opportunities to learn, most young people grow into thoughtful adults. In the meantime, a little understanding on both sides can make life at home easier.

paras.A: Deserts cover about a third of the Earth's land surface. They are defined not by heat but by dryness: any region that receives less than 250 millimetres of rain a year is a desert, whether it is as hot as the Sahara or as cold as the Gobi in winter. Life there is difficult, but it is far from absent. Plants, animals and people have found remarkable ways to survive.
paras.B: Plants face the greatest challenge, since they cannot move to find water. Many have developed deep roots that reach water far below the surface, while others have shallow roots that spread widely to catch a brief rain. Cacti store water in their thick stems and have spines instead of leaves, reducing the loss of moisture. Some desert plants lie dormant as seeds for years, and after a rare downpour, they sprout, flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks, covering the sand in colour.
paras.C: Animals use different strategies. Many avoid the heat by staying in burrows during the day and emerging at night. The fennec fox has huge ears that lose heat, and the kangaroo rat can live without drinking, as it obtains the water it needs from the seeds it eats. Camels, famous for their endurance, can lose a quarter of their body weight in water and recover it in a few minutes of drinking. Lizards and snakes control their temperature by moving between sun and shade.
paras.D: People have also adapted. Nomadic peoples such as the Bedouin and the Tuareg follow the rains with herds of camels and goats, and their loose robes protect the skin from the sun while allowing air to circulate. Houses in desert towns of Central Asia and the Middle East are built from thick clay walls that stay cool in the day and warm at night, and many have inner courtyards with trees and small pools. Underground canals, called qanats or karez, bring water from distant mountains without losing it to evaporation.
paras.E: Modern technology has changed life in dry lands. Wells and pipes bring water to remote areas, and irrigation has turned some deserts into farmland. However, this success has a cost: taking too much from underground reserves can lower the water table and dry up the oases that people have depended on for centuries. The Aral Sea disaster is a warning of what can happen when the limits of a dry environment are ignored.
paras.F: Still, deserts have much to teach us. The people and creatures who live in them show that with care, knowledge and respect for limits, survival is possible even in the harshest places. As the world warms and dry lands expand, these lessons may become more valuable.

paras.A: Every day, thousands of tonnes of material from space fall towards the Earth. Most of it consists of tiny grains of dust that burn up in the atmosphere, producing the brief streaks of light we call shooting stars. Occasionally, a larger piece survives the journey and lands on the ground. Such a rock is called a meteorite, and scientists treasure them as free samples of the early solar system.
paras.B: Most meteorites come from the asteroid belt, a region between Mars and Jupiter containing millions of rocky bodies. These objects are leftovers from the formation of the planets, about four and a half billion years ago. Because they have changed very little, they offer a direct view of the conditions at that time. A few meteorites have been identified as pieces of the Moon or Mars, thrown into space by ancient impacts.
paras.C: There are three main types. Stony meteorites, the most common, resemble Earth rocks, although they contain tiny round grains that are older than anything found on the Earth's surface. Iron meteorites, made of metal, are dense and heavy, and for centuries, they were prized as a source of iron: the Egyptian ruler Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger made from meteoric iron. Stony-iron meteorites are rare, and when polished, they can be beautiful.
paras.D: Some meteorites contain surprising ingredients. In 1969, a stone that fell near the Australian town of Murchison was found to contain amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. This supported the idea that some of the chemicals necessary for life may have arrived on Earth from space. The question of whether life itself could have come this way remains unanswered, but the discovery changed the way scientists think about our origins.
paras.E: Most visitors are small, but a few have been enormous. About sixty-six million years ago, an object roughly ten kilometres wide struck what is now Mexico, and the resulting dust and fires changed the climate so dramatically that the dinosaurs and many other species became extinct. A smaller body exploded over Siberia in 1908 and flattened millions of trees across an area bigger than a large city. In 2013, a smaller explosion over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk broke thousands of windows and injured over a thousand people.
paras.F: Today, astronomers use telescopes to search for large objects near our planet and calculate their orbits. So far, none is known to threaten the Earth in the near future. Space agencies have even tested whether a spacecraft could change the path of an asteroid by crashing into it. The experiment succeeded, offering hope that, if a dangerous object were ever discovered early enough, humans might be able to protect their planet.
