paras.A: Fish are an important source of protein for more than three billion people, and the fishing industry employs tens of millions. Yet scientists warn that many of the world's fish populations are being caught faster than they can reproduce. According to some estimates, about a third of the world's fish stocks are fished at unsustainable levels, and in several regions, once-common species have almost disappeared.
paras.B: The causes are not hard to find. Modern fishing boats are equipped with sonar, which detects fish, and with giant nets that can take thousands of tonnes in a single trip. Fleets from rich countries travel across oceans to waters near poorer ones, where local fishermen in small boats cannot compete. In addition, some vessels fish illegally, ignoring catch limits and sailing without a licence, which makes the task of managing stocks even harder.
paras.C: Many fishing methods also damage the environment. Trawling, in which a heavy net is dragged along the sea floor, destroys habitats such as coral and sponges. Nets intended for one species catch other animals by accident, and these 'bycatch' animals, including turtles, dolphins and sharks, are often thrown back dead. Scientists estimate that millions of tonnes of unwanted fish are discarded each year.
paras.D: There are practical solutions. Governments can set catch limits based on scientific advice, create no-fishing zones where stocks can recover and punish illegal operators. In some regions, these steps have already worked: after strict rules were introduced in the waters of the North Atlantic, populations of several species of cod and herring recovered within a decade. Technology also helps, as satellites can track vessels and reveal those that turn off their position signals.
paras.E: Consumers play a role as well. Labels now indicate whether fish comes from a sustainable source, and shoppers can choose these products. Eating a greater variety of species, rather than the few most popular, also reduces pressure on the best-known stocks. Some people choose to eat fish less often, and others turn to fish farms, although fish farming raises its own problems, including pollution and the use of wild fish as feed.
paras.F: The future of fishing depends on cooperation between governments, industry and consumers. If the fish are protected today, they will supply food and income for generations. If they are not, the sea may become a place of empty nets, with consequences for millions of families.

paras.A: 'All roads lead to Rome,' says the proverb, and it was almost true. At its largest, the Roman Empire had a network of paved roads of about eighty thousand kilometres, linking cities from Britain to the Middle East. These roads were not built for travellers' comfort. Their first purpose was military: they allowed soldiers to move quickly to any threatened frontier, and an army could march about thirty kilometres a day along them.
paras.B: Roman engineers built roads in a systematic way. First, surveyors chose the most direct route, using simple instruments to keep the line straight over long distances. Then workers dug a trench and filled it with several layers: large stones at the bottom, smaller stones and gravel above, and finally flat paving stones on top. The surface was curved slightly so that rainwater ran off into ditches on either side. This construction was so solid that many roads were still in use more than a thousand years later.
paras.C: The roads served many purposes besides war. Officials used them to carry orders and taxes, and a postal system with relay stations allowed messages to travel about fifty kilometres in a day, and more in emergencies. Merchants carried goods from one province to another, and the movement of trade increased the wealth of the empire. Every few kilometres, milestones displayed the distance to the nearest city, and inns offered food and rest to travellers.
paras.D: The effects on daily life were great. Because transport became cheaper and safer, food, pottery and wine could be exchanged across great distances. A person in northern Britain could eat olives from Spain. Ideas travelled too: roads helped to spread Latin, new religions and Roman customs. Many modern European highways follow the lines of the old routes, and numerous towns grew where roads crossed.
paras.E: The roads also had drawbacks. The same routes that carried Roman legions later carried invading armies, and as the empire weakened, enemies used the roads to reach the heart of the state. The cost of maintenance was heavy, and when the central government could no longer pay for repairs, the roads fell into disrepair. In many regions, travel became slow and dangerous.
paras.F: Despite this, the achievement of the Roman engineers remains impressive. They showed that a state which invests in transport can unite distant regions and encourage trade. It is no accident that many modern governments, from China to the European Union, have again made roads and railways a priority.

title: The Great Rivers of Central Asia

paras.A: Central Asia is mostly dry, but two great rivers cross it: the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. For thousands of years, they have shaped the history, agriculture and culture of the region. Both rise in high mountains, fed by melting snow and glaciers, and flow north-west across deserts to the Aral Sea. Without them, there would be no cities such as Bukhara, Khiva or Termez.
paras.B: The Amu Darya, about 2,500 kilometres long, is the larger. In antiquity, it was known to the Greeks as the Oxus, and it formed a natural frontier between the Persian world and the nomadic peoples of the north. Along its banks lay the ancient kingdoms of Khorezm and Bactria, whose farmers dug canals to bring water to the fields. The river changes its course often, because its banks are soft; in the past, entire cities were abandoned when it moved away.
paras.C: The Syr Darya, known to the Greeks as the Jaxartes, is longer, at about 2,200 kilometres from its sources, but carries less water. It flows through the Fergana Valley, where it irrigates cotton, rice and fruit orchards, and then crosses the steppe of Kazakhstan. Historically it marked the line between settled farmers and herders, and many battles were fought on its shores.
paras.D: Both rivers were central to trade. Boats carried goods along them, and the caravan routes of the Silk Road often followed their valleys. Towns on the rivers grew rich from customs duties and from supplying food and water to merchants. Poets praised the rivers' beauty, and travellers described the green oases that appeared like islands in a sea of sand.
paras.E: In the twentieth century, the use of the rivers changed dramatically. Huge canals were built to irrigate cotton, and the amount of water reaching the Aral Sea declined year by year. By the 1990s, the lake that had been the fourth largest in the world had lost most of its water. Today the three states along the rivers must share them, and the matter requires careful agreements, since upstream countries need water for electricity while downstream ones need it for farming.
paras.F: The challenge for the future is to balance these needs. Modern technologies, such as drip irrigation and lined canals, can reduce waste, and regional cooperation is growing. If wisely managed, the great rivers can continue to support millions of people. If not, the region may face shortages that no map can fix.

paras.A: In 1609, an Italian scientist named Galileo Galilei heard about a Dutch invention that made distant objects appear closer. He built his own version, improved it and turned it towards the sky. What he saw changed our view of the universe for ever. The Moon was not a smooth, perfect sphere but a world with mountains and craters. The Milky Way was not a cloud but a vast collection of stars. And around the planet Jupiter, he found four small points of light that moved night after night: they were moons.
paras.B: These discoveries shook the accepted wisdom. For centuries, scholars had taught that everything in the heavens revolved around the Earth. Galileo's observation of moons circling Jupiter showed that not everything did. He also saw that Venus has phases like the Moon, which supported the theory that the planets orbit the Sun. His support for this idea brought him into conflict with the Church, and in 1633, he was forced to deny his belief and spend the remainder of his life under house arrest.
paras.C: Telescopes improved quickly. Galileo's instrument used lenses, but lenses suffer from coloured edges, and large ones are heavy and hard to make. In the 1660s, Isaac Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror instead, which avoided these problems. Almost all large modern telescopes use mirrors. The largest today have mirrors more than ten metres wide, made from many separate pieces that work together as one.
paras.D: The next revolution was to look at light we cannot see. Stars and galaxies also emit radio waves, infrared light, X-rays and gamma rays, and special telescopes reveal sights hidden to the eye. Radio telescopes discovered pulsars, the rapidly spinning remains of exploded stars, and microwaves that survive from the early universe. Some of these instruments are placed in orbit, since the atmosphere blocks many types of radiation.
paras.E: The most famous space telescope is Hubble, launched in 1990. Free from the blurring effect of the air, it has taken pictures of galaxies billions of light years away and helped to measure the age of the universe. Its successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, which began operating in 2022, is designed to see even further back in time, to when the first stars formed.
paras.F: Telescopes have taught us that our planet is a very small part of a vast cosmos. They have found thousands of planets circling other stars, and some of these may be similar to Earth. Whether life exists on any of them remains a mystery, but the search that Galileo began with a small tube of glass and a curiosity about the sky continues.

paras.A: Laughter is one of the first sounds a baby makes, usually at around four months, long before it can speak. All human cultures laugh, and the sound is remarkably similar across the world. Even deaf and blind children laugh without having heard or seen anyone doing it. This suggests that laughter is not learned but built into us, an ancient part of what it means to be human.
paras.B: Surprisingly, laughter probably began long before humour. Researchers who study apes have found that chimpanzees and gorillas make a breathy, panting sound when they are tickled or when they play, and this sound is thought to be the ancestor of human laughter. Its original purpose seems to have been social: to signal that rough play is friendly and not a fight. In humans, laughter retained this function.
paras.C: In fact, most laughter has little to do with jokes. When scientists recorded conversations, they found that people laughed far more often in response to ordinary remarks such as 'I'll see you later' than in response to comic ones. The laughter acted as a signal of friendliness, agreement or a wish to keep the conversation smooth. People also laugh about thirty times more often when they are with others than when they are alone.

paras.F: Whatever its exact purpose, laughter is a powerful social tool. It builds bonds, relieves tension and makes difficult situations easier. Perhaps that is why we trust people with a good sense of humour, and why a shared joke can make strangers feel like friends within minutes.

paras.A: For most of human history, cities were places of stone, smoke and crowds, and parks were luxuries for the rich. Today, as more than half of the world's population lives in urban areas, planners and doctors increasingly agree that green space is not a decoration but a necessity. Trees, gardens and parks improve the quality of life of city residents in several ways.
paras.B: The first benefit is health. People who live near green areas tend to exercise more, and studies suggest they suffer less from stress and depression. In one experiment, volunteers who walked for an hour in a forest showed lower levels of a stress hormone than those who walked along a busy street. Hospitals report that patients with a view of trees often recover faster and need less pain medicine than those who look at a wall.
paras.C: Green space also cools the city. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat, and in summer, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the 'urban heat island'. Trees provide shade, and as water evaporates from leaves, the air is cooled. A street lined with large trees can be up to ten degrees cooler than a bare one, which can save lives during heatwaves and reduce the need for air conditioning.
paras.D: Plants help to clean the air and control floods. Leaves trap dust and absorb some pollution, while soil in parks and gardens soaks up rainwater that would otherwise run into the drains. Some cities are creating 'green roofs' covered with grass or plants, which insulate buildings and slow the flow of water. Parks and rivers can also provide homes for birds, bees and butterflies, helping nature to survive among the buildings.
paras.E: Of course, green space costs money and takes land that could be used for housing. Not everyone has equal access: in many cities, wealthy districts have large parks while poorer ones have almost none. Some planners respond by creating small spaces, such as pocket parks on empty plots, and by planting trees along streets. Community gardens, where neighbours grow vegetables together, can also bring people closer.
paras.F: The evidence suggests that investment in green space repays itself through better health, lower energy bills and happier residents. The question for future cities is not whether to have nature, but how to share it fairly. The best cities of tomorrow may be those where nobody lives more than a short walk from a tree.

paras.A: According to a popular legend, coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating the red berries of a certain bush. Whether or not the story is true, coffee plants did originate in the highlands of Ethiopia. By the fifteenth century, people in Yemen were roasting the beans and drinking the dark liquid, mainly to stay awake during long hours of prayer and study.
paras.B: From Arabia, coffee spread to Cairo, Istanbul and the cities of Persia. Coffee houses opened, and they soon became places where men gathered to talk, play chess and listen to music. Some rulers worried that these meeting places encouraged criticism of the government, and they occasionally closed them. Yet the custom was too popular to stop, and the coffee house became an important part of city life across the region.
paras.C: Merchants from Venice brought coffee to Europe in the seventeenth century. At first, some people called it the 'bitter invention of Satan', but according to a well-known story the Pope tasted it and approved. Coffee houses in London were called 'penny universities' because for the price of one penny a customer could buy a cup and listen to educated conversation. Several famous businesses, including an insurance market, began in such places.
paras.D: Today, coffee is grown in more than fifty countries, mostly in a belt around the equator. Brazil produces the largest amount, followed by Vietnam and Colombia. The plants need warmth, rain and shade, and the best beans are often picked by hand from trees on mountain slopes. Millions of small farmers depend on the crop for their income, and when the price falls, their families suffer.
paras.E: Coffee is now one of the most traded products in the world, and billions of cups are drunk every day. Scientists believe that moderate amounts, about three or four cups a day, are safe for most adults, although too much can cause sleeplessness and a fast heartbeat. Many buyers now choose coffee labelled 'fair trade', which promises farmers a minimum price for their beans.
paras.F: The way coffee is prepared has also changed over the centuries. Early drinkers boiled the ground beans in a pot, producing a thick, strong drink. Italian engineers later invented machines that force hot water through the coffee under pressure, and these made the quick, small cup known as espresso popular. In recent years, many cafes have begun to treat coffee almost like wine, describing the farm, the height of the land and the flavours of each batch to customers who are happy to pay more.

paras.A: A glacier is a huge river of ice that moves very slowly down a valley or across land. It forms where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Over many years, the snow is pressed into ice by its own weight, and eventually the ice begins to flow under the force of gravity. Today, glaciers cover about ten per cent of the Earth's land, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland.
paras.B: Glaciers shape the landscape in dramatic ways. As they move, they carry rocks that scrape the ground beneath like sandpaper, carving deep valleys with steep sides. When a glacier melts, it leaves behind lakes, ridges of rubble and the U-shaped valleys that are common in mountain regions such as Switzerland and Norway. Some of the most beautiful scenery in the world was created in this way.
paras.C: Glaciers are also vital stores of fresh water. About two-thirds of the world's fresh water is frozen in ice, and in many regions, rivers are fed by melting glaciers in summer. In parts of Central Asia, the Andes and the Himalayas, farmers and cities depend on this meltwater when rain is scarce. The glaciers act like a bank, saving water in winter and releasing it when it is needed most.
paras.D: Unfortunately, most glaciers are now shrinking. Measurements over the last fifty years show that mountain glaciers have lost enormous amounts of ice, and the speed of the loss is increasing. Scientists link the change to rising temperatures caused by human activity. Some small glaciers have already disappeared completely, and photographs taken a century apart show shocking differences.
paras.E: The consequences are serious. In the short term, extra meltwater can cause floods when lakes behind natural walls of rock suddenly burst. In the long term, there will be less water for rivers, and the ice that melts from land adds to the rise of the sea. Researchers continue to study glaciers closely, and many believe that reducing pollution is the only way to slow the loss.
paras.F: Visitors can still see the power of glaciers in many places. Tourists walk on the ice in Iceland and New Zealand, and guides explain how the ice has moved and changed. These trips are popular and bring money to mountain villages, but they also create a dilemma, since the travel needed to reach the glaciers produces pollution that helps to melt them. Some local people therefore ask that visits be limited and that guides teach visitors about the fragile world they have come to admire.

paras.A: The surface of the Earth is not one solid piece. It is broken into huge plates of rock that slowly move, at about the speed at which fingernails grow. Most of the time, the movement is too slow to feel. But where two plates meet, they can become stuck, and the pressure builds for years or even centuries.
paras.B: When the pressure becomes too great, the rock suddenly slips, and energy is released as waves that travel through the ground. This is an earthquake. The point underground where the slip begins is called the focus, and the place directly above it on the surface is the epicentre. Strong shaking is usually felt most near the epicentre, though soft ground can magnify the movement farther away.
paras.C: Scientists measure earthquakes with instruments called seismometers. For many years, the Richter scale was used to give a number for the size of a quake. Today, experts prefer a more accurate system, the moment magnitude scale. Each step up the scale means about thirty-two times more energy, so a quake of magnitude 7 is vastly more powerful than one of magnitude 5.
paras.D: Damage depends on more than size. Buildings made of unreinforced brick or stone are the most dangerous, because they can collapse and trap people. In contrast, modern buildings with flexible steel frames can sway without falling. Earthquakes under the sea may also push up huge waves called tsunamis, which can travel across an ocean and strike coasts far from the source.
paras.E: At present, nobody can predict exactly when and where an earthquake will happen. Scientists can say which areas are at greatest risk, and some countries have set up warning systems that give people a few seconds of notice after the first waves are detected. Even a few seconds can be enough to stop trains, open fire-station doors and let people take cover.
paras.F: Ordinary people can prepare for an earthquake in simple ways. Experts advise families to fasten tall furniture to the wall, to keep a bag with water, food and a torch near the door, and to agree on a meeting place. During shaking, the safest action is usually to drop to the floor, cover the head and hold on to something solid, rather than run outside, where falling objects are a danger. Schools in earthquake regions often practise these steps so that children react automatically.

paras.A: Yellowstone, in the United States, was made a national park in 1872. It was the first in the world, and its geysers, forests and valleys are famous. But by the 1920s, one important animal had disappeared from it. Wolves had been hunted by farmers and hunters until none remained, because people feared them and believed they killed too many sheep and deer.
paras.B: In the decades that followed, the number of elk, a large kind of deer, grew rapidly. Without wolves to hunt them, the elk ate huge quantities of young trees and bushes along the rivers. The willows and aspens failed to grow back, and with fewer trees, beavers lost their food and their building materials. The park slowly became poorer in plants and animals.
paras.C: In 1995, after years of argument, scientists brought thirty-one wolves from Canada and released them in the park. The results were remarkable. The wolves hunted elk, but they also changed the way elk behaved. The deer avoided open valleys where they could be attacked, and moved around more. In places where they had been grazing for years, young trees began to grow again.
paras.D: As the willows returned, so did the beavers, and their dams created ponds where fish, frogs and birds could live. Songbirds nested in the taller trees, and even the riverbanks became steadier because roots held the soil. Some scientists call this a 'trophic cascade': a change at the top of the food chain that spreads downward through the whole natural system.
paras.E: Not everyone agrees that wolves were the only cause of these changes, since weather and other animals also play a part. Farmers near the park still worry about their cattle. Yet most researchers accept that the return of the wolves has helped the park, and the story is often used to explain why healthy nature needs predators.
paras.F: The story of Yellowstone has also changed the way people think about conservation. In the past, protecting nature often meant protecting only the animals that people liked, such as deer. Today, many managers try to protect whole systems, including the predators, insects and plants that depend on one another. Other countries have considered returning wolves, lynx or bears to places they once lived, though each plan must balance the needs of wildlife with the worries of the people who live nearby.

paras.A: Our bodies have a defence system called the immune system. When a harmful germ, such as a virus, enters the body, white blood cells attack it and learn to recognise it. The first time, this takes several days, and the person may become ill. But the body remembers the germ, so that if it returns, the defence is much faster.
paras.B: A vaccine uses this memory without the illness. It contains a harmless piece or weakened form of the germ, or instructions that teach cells to make a harmless piece. The body reacts as though it were attacked, and builds a store of memory cells. If the real germ ever arrives, the immune system is ready, and the disease is either prevented or becomes much milder.
paras.C: The idea is old. In the 1790s, Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught the mild disease cowpox seemed protected from smallpox. He tested his idea on a boy, and the practice spread around the world. Later, Louis Pasteur created vaccines against rabies and other diseases. Smallpox was finally declared gone in 1980, the only human disease to have been completely removed.
paras.D: Vaccines protect not only the person who receives them but also the community. When most people are immune, a disease finds it hard to spread, and those who cannot be vaccinated, such as very young babies, are protected indirectly. Doctors call this 'herd immunity'. The more contagious the disease, the greater the share of people who need to be vaccinated to achieve it.
paras.E: Vaccines, like all medicines, can have side effects, but these are usually mild, such as a sore arm or a slight fever. Serious reactions are extremely rare. Despite the evidence of their safety, false rumours spread quickly on the internet and make some parents afraid. Health workers try to answer such fears with patience and clear facts.
paras.F: The development of a new vaccine is a long process. Researchers first test an idea in the laboratory, then on animals, and finally on volunteers in three stages, involving at first a few dozen and later many thousands of people. At each step, independent experts check whether the vaccine is safe and whether it works. Even after approval, doctors continue to record any problems. In an emergency, the stages can be done at the same time, which saves months, but none of the checks is skipped.

paras.A: Plastic is cheap, light and strong, and for these reasons it has become one of the most useful materials ever invented. It is used for bottles, bags, toys, phones and parts of cars. But the qualities that make it useful also create a problem. Plastic does not rot like wood or paper, and a single bottle can remain in the environment for hundreds of years.
paras.B: Each year, millions of tonnes of plastic waste reach the sea. Some is dropped by careless people, but much is carried by rivers or blown from rubbish dumps. In certain parts of the ocean, currents gather the waste into slowly turning areas known as 'garbage patches'. The largest, between Hawaii and California, is thought to be several times the size of France, though it is not a solid island, as some people imagine.
paras.C: Marine animals suffer greatly. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed pieces of plastic to their chicks. Others become trapped in old fishing nets and drown. Over time, the sun and waves break large pieces into tiny fragments called microplastics, which are eaten by small creatures and may travel up the food chain to fish that people eat.
paras.D: Solutions are being tried at many levels. Several countries have banned thin plastic bags or put a small charge on them, and the number of bags used has fallen sharply. Engineers are developing materials that break down naturally, and some companies collect fishing nets to turn them into carpets. Volunteers organise beach clean-ups, which, besides removing rubbish, raise awareness.
paras.E: Experts agree, however, that clean-ups alone are not enough, since more plastic enters the sea every day. The most effective approach is to reduce the amount produced in the first place, to reuse items and to recycle properly. Individuals can help by choosing products with less packaging and refusing things they do not need.
paras.F: Some young inventors have offered creative ideas. One teenager designed a floating barrier to collect waste from rivers before it reaches the sea, and others have made bricks, paving stones and even clothing from recycled plastic. Not every idea works on a large scale, and critics warn that technology cannot replace changes in the way we shop and throw away goods. Still, such projects show that many people are willing to take the problem seriously and look for practical answers.

paras.A: Whales are the largest animals that have ever lived. The blue whale can grow to thirty metres in length and weigh as much as two hundred tonnes, and its heart is about the size of a small car. Although whales live in the sea, they are not fish. They are mammals, which means that they breathe air, give birth to live young and feed their babies with milk.
paras.B: Whales belong to two main groups. Baleen whales, such as the humpback and the blue whale, have no teeth. Instead, they have long plates in their mouths that act like a sieve, filtering out tiny shrimp-like creatures called krill. Toothed whales, which include dolphins and the sperm whale, hunt fish and squid. The sperm whale can dive more than a kilometre below the surface in search of its food.
paras.C: Sound is vital to whales, because light does not travel far in deep water. Toothed whales use clicks to find their way and locate prey, a method known as echolocation: the sound bounces back from an object, and the whale judges its size and distance from the echo. Baleen whales communicate with long, low calls that can travel for hundreds of kilometres in some conditions.
paras.D: The most famous sounds are the songs of male humpback whales. A song can last up to twenty minutes and is repeated for hours. Remarkably, all the males in one area sing the same song, and it slowly changes from year to year. Sometimes a new song spreads across the ocean, from one group to the next, in the way that a popular tune spreads among people.
paras.E: Hunting nearly destroyed many species. In the twentieth century, hundreds of thousands of whales were killed for their oil and meat, and some populations fell to a tiny fraction of their original size. An international agreement stopped most commercial hunting in 1986, and several species, including the humpback, have since recovered well, although a few remain in danger.
paras.F: Today, whales face new threats. Ships can collide with them, fishing nets can trap them, and noise from engines can disturb their communication. Scientists are working with shipping companies to change routes in busy whale areas and to design quieter propellers. Whale watching also brings income to coastal towns, which gives local people a reason to protect the animals.

paras.A: The sun delivers more energy to the Earth in one hour than the whole of humanity uses in a year. The problem has always been how to collect and use it. paras.C: Solar power suits both large and small projects. Giant solar farms in deserts can supply whole cities. At the same time, a family can put a few panels on the roof of its house, and in places far from power lines, a single panel can run lights, a radio and a phone charger. paras.E: Governments can encourage the change in several ways. paras.A: A generation ago, most people bought clothes a few times a year and expected them to last. Today, many shops offer new styles every week at very low prices, so that a shirt can cost less than a sandwich. This business model, known as 'fast fashion', copies ideas from the catwalk and produces them quickly in large numbers.
paras.B: For customers, the attraction is obvious: they can follow trends cheaply. However, clothes made in this way are often poorly stitched and are worn only a few times. Surveys suggest that the average item is thrown away after being worn seven to ten times, and in some countries, a truck load of textiles is sent to a rubbish dump every second.
paras.C: The environmental cost is large. Growing cotton needs great amounts of water, and one cotton shirt may take thousands of litres to produce. Dyes from factories can pollute rivers, and washing synthetic clothes releases tiny fibres of plastic that end up in the sea. In total, the fashion industry is estimated to cause several per cent of the world's greenhouse gas emissions.
paras.D: There is also a human cost. Many garments are sewn in countries where wages are low, and factory workers may face long hours and unsafe buildings. A factory collapse in Bangladesh in 2013, which killed more than a thousand people, shocked the world and led to new safety agreements, but campaigners say that progress has been uneven.
paras.E: Alternatives are growing. Second-hand shops and online resale sites let people buy good clothes cheaply and keep them out of the rubbish. Some brands offer repair services or make garments from recycled fibres, and more people are organising clothes swaps with friends. A simple guide is to buy fewer items of better quality and wear them for years.
paras.F: Change must come from several directions at once. Governments could require clothing to be labelled with its environmental impact, companies could be responsible for collecting what they sell, and shoppers could ask whether they truly need another item. Fashion will always be fun, but it need not be so wasteful. Some designers also argue that clothes should be treated like furniture or tools, as valuable things that deserve care. If more people shared this view, shops would sell fewer items, but each item would last longer and carry a fairer price.

paras.A: Many people believe that only children can learn a language well, and it is true that young learners often copy sounds more naturally. Adults, however, have important advantages. They understand grammar rules, they can use study skills, and they know how to connect new words with what they already know. With the right approach, an adult can make steady progress.
paras.B: One of the most important factors is time spent in contact with the language. Studies suggest that the learners who improve fastest are those who use the language every day, even for short periods. Twenty minutes of reading, listening or speaking daily generally works better than a single long session once a week, because the brain consolidates new information during rest.
paras.C: Motivation also matters. People who have a clear reason, such as a job, a friendship or a journey, tend to persist longer than those who study only because they must. Enjoyment helps too. Learners who watch films, listen to songs or read stories in the new language often notice that they pick up words without trying, since interesting material holds attention.
paras.D: Fear of mistakes can be a serious obstacle. Some learners remain silent for months because they want every sentence to be perfect. Teachers point out that errors are a normal and necessary part of learning, and that speaking, even badly, offers the practice that no book can supply. A friendly partner who will listen without laughing is often worth more than an expensive course.
paras.E: Technology has made learning easier. Apps offer short daily exercises, online tutors allow conversations with native speakers across the world, and subtitles on videos link spoken and written forms. Nevertheless, tools alone are not enough. The learner must still decide to practise, and no program can do the thinking for them.
paras.F: Learning a second language brings rewards beyond communication. Research suggests that bilingual people are often better at switching attention between tasks, and that speaking two languages may help the brain remain healthy in old age. Perhaps the greatest reward is a new view of the world, since every language describes it in a slightly different way. Whatever the reason for learning, the process takes patience. Most experts agree that reaching a comfortable level takes months or years rather than weeks, and that the learners who succeed are usually those who keep going when progress feels slow.

paras.A: Cooking is chemistry that we can eat. When we heat food, the substances inside it change, and these changes make food safer, softer and more flavourful. Understanding some of the science helps cooks to avoid disasters and to invent new dishes with confidence.
paras.B: One of the best-known reactions is browning. When bread is toasted or meat is fried, sugars and proteins on the surface react at high temperatures to create hundreds of new flavours and a golden colour. This is called the Maillard reaction, after the French scientist who described it. It does not happen well in a wet pan, which is why cooks dry meat before frying it.
paras.C: Heat also changes proteins. In an egg, the proteins unwind and join together as the temperature rises, turning a clear liquid into a solid. If the egg is heated for too long, the proteins squeeze out the water and become rubbery. The same principle explains why overcooked meat is tough, and why gentle cooking at a low temperature can produce very tender results.
paras.D: Bread depends on living organisms. Yeast, a tiny fungus, feeds on the sugar in dough and releases bubbles of gas. The gas is trapped by a stretchy network formed by a protein in flour, and the dough rises. When the loaf is baked, the heat kills the yeast and sets the structure, leaving a light, airy centre and a crisp crust.
paras.E: Salt, acid and fat play different parts. Salt strengthens flavours, and a little lemon juice or vinegar can brighten a heavy dish. Fat carries flavours, which dissolve in it more easily than in water, and gives food a smooth feeling in the mouth. Professional chefs balance these elements almost without thinking.
paras.F: Cooking is also a safety matter. Heat kills most of the harmful bacteria in meat, eggs and rice, but food left for hours in a warm kitchen allows germs to multiply. Keeping raw and cooked foods apart and chilling leftovers quickly are simple rules that prevent many illnesses. Many cooks today enjoy learning why a recipe works. A little curiosity turns the daily task of preparing a meal into a small experiment, and the results can usually be tasted straight away. Even simple habits, such as washing hands and using clean boards and knives, make a large difference to the safety of what we eat.

paras.A: Since the earliest times, people have needed to cross rivers and valleys. The first bridges were probably fallen trees or flat stones laid across a stream. As societies grew, these simple crossings developed into impressive structures that have shaped trade, war and travel.
paras.B: There are three basic types. A beam bridge is the simplest: a flat platform supported at each end and sometimes in the middle. An arch bridge curves upward, and the weight is pushed outward along the curve to the supports at each end. A suspension bridge hangs its deck from thick cables stretched between tall towers, which makes it suitable for very long gaps.
paras.C: The Romans were master builders of arches. Many of their stone bridges and aqueducts are still standing after two thousand years, because the arch shape keeps the stones pressed tightly together. In China, builders constructed graceful bridges with a single high arch, and in the Islamic world, caravan roads were crossed by sturdy bridges which served merchants for centuries.
paras.D: The Industrial Revolution brought iron and steel. In 1779, the world's first iron bridge was built in England, and by the nineteenth century, engineers could build long suspension bridges with steel cables. The Brooklyn Bridge in New York, completed in 1883, was for a time the longest in the world and became a symbol of the city.
paras.E: Building a bridge is difficult. Engineers must calculate the weight of the structure and the loads it will carry, then allow for wind, floods and earthquakes. In 1940, a bridge in the United States twisted violently in a moderate wind and collapsed, and the failure taught designers to test models in wind tunnels.
paras.F: Today, the longest bridges span many kilometres and use computers in design. Yet the important principles are old. A good bridge must be strong, economical and, if possible, beautiful. People often love their bridges: they are meeting places, landmarks and in many cities, the pride of the people who live near them. New materials, such as strong plastics and lighter concrete, are being tested, and engineers are also designing bridges with sensors that report damage early, so that repairs can be made before an accident can occur. Many old bridges are now protected as monuments, and cities spend large sums to repair them, because their value to history is as great as their value to traffic.
